title: Project manager, project support and agile coach
blurb: Explain the responsibilities of the project manager, project support and agile coach, and pick the right one for a situation.
question: A board member keeps resisting the move to dashboards and wants weekly written reports. Which role should help remove this blocker to agile adoption?

teach.body: The project manager runs the project day to day on behalf of the project board, within agreed tolerances and constraints. Project support gives administrative and specialist help so the project runs smoothly. The agile coach is a mentor and facilitator who helps the organization adopt and sustain agile principles and practices, working across teams rather than inside one.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, Table B.1

Works at

teach.h: Project manager: servant leader within tolerances
teach.body: The PM has the authority to run the project for the board within the agreed tolerances. They act as a servant leader, linking governance and the delivery teams. They agree work package descriptions (sets of user stories) with product owners, consult product owners and stakeholders on product backlogs and management approaches, and make sure risks are identified, assessed and controlled. They do not prioritize across teams.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, Table B.1

teach.body: Project support provides administrative support tailored to agile iterations and workshops, advice on project tools, and planning, risk and change management support. It helps meet reporting needs by updating and pulling information from project and team dashboards, assists with stakeholder analysis and documentation, compiles lists, and helps communication flow between governance roles and teams.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table B.1

teach.h: Agile coach: change across the organization
teach.body: The agile coach works across teams to identify and remove systemic blockers to agile adoption, such as a senior manager resisting dashboards. They support the board, project assurance and the PM with expert agile knowledge, and help embed agile ways of working into the project's approaches. A role description might state that the PM is mentored by the agile coach. Early in a transformation the coach builds knowledge through training and on-the-job coaching.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, Table B.1, 2.7.3

teach.body: Pennant Rail is replacing its ticket machines. Project manager Kofi Asante agrees sets of user stories with the two product owners and keeps the risk register under control. Support officer Grace Liddell runs workshop logistics, keeps the dashboards current and drafts the stakeholder list. When finance director Neil Dunmore insists on long written reports, agile coach Saanvi Rao works with him and the board so that dashboards meet his needs.

teach.text: The agile coach works at ORGANIZATION level on systemic blockers; the team coach works inside one or two teams. And the agile coach does not prioritize user stories or do admin: priorities belong to the CPO and POs, admin to project support.

items: PM: runs the project day to day for the board within tolerances.
PM: servant leader; agrees work packages with POs; makes sure risks are controlled.
Project support: admin for iterations and workshops, tools advice, dashboards, lists.
Project support assists stakeholder analysis and communication between governance and teams.
Agile coach: removes systemic blockers across teams; supports board, assurance and PM.
Agile coach is not a team-level role and does not prioritize the backlog.

summary: You can now explain what the project manager, project support and agile coach each do. You can also choose between them, and tell the agile coach from the team coach and support from assurance.

A.q: Which role runs the project day to day on behalf of the project board?
A.why: The PM has the authority to run the project on behalf of the board within the agreed tolerances and constraints (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: The executive is accountable for the project at governance level, not its daily running.
whyNot.2: The CPO represents users and prioritizes across teams.
whyNot.3: The agile coach mentors and facilitates agile adoption across the organization.

A.q: Which role updates and pulls information from the project and team dashboards to meet reporting needs?
A.why: Project support helps manage reporting requirements by updating and pulling information from project and team dashboards (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: Assurance monitors adherence to principles and practices rather than maintaining dashboards.
whyNot.1: The team coach helps teams self-manage and facilitates team workshops.
whyNot.2: The agile coach removes systemic blockers and supports leaders with expert knowledge.

A.q: What is the agile coach's main focus?
options: Helping the organization adopt and sustain agile
Owning the product backlog for a delivery team
Agreeing work package descriptions with POs
Testing products against the Definition of Done
A.why: The agile coach is a mentor and facilitator who helps organizations adopt and sustain agile principles and practices (Table 7.2).

whyNot.1: Owning a team's product backlog is the product owner's job.
whyNot.2: Agreeing work packages with POs is the project manager's job.
whyNot.3: Testing against the DoD is the tester's job.

B.q: A project director is resisting agile reporting and wants detailed weekly documents. Which role should work to remove this blocker?
B.why: The agile coach works across teams to identify and remove systemic blockers to agile adoption (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: Project support could produce reports, but that would not tackle the resistance itself.
whyNot.1: Assurance monitors adherence; it does not coach leaders through resistance.
whyNot.3: The team coach works inside one or two teams, not with senior leaders.

B.q: Which role gives administrative support tailored to agile iterations and workshops?
B.why: Project support provides administrative support tailored to agile iterations and workshops (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The PM leads the project day to day and is supported by project support.
whyNot.1: The agile coach gives expert agile knowledge, not administrative support.
whyNot.2: The PO leads a delivery team and owns its backlog.

B.q:
Which two statements about the project manager are correct?
1. The PM acts as a servant leader linking governance and teams.
2. The PM sets priorities across all delivery teams.
3. The PM makes sure risks are identified, assessed and controlled.
4. The PM directly manages each developer's daily tasks.
B.why: The PM is a servant leader between governance and teams (1) and makes sure project risks are identified, assessed and controlled (3) (Table B.1).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is wrong: the CPO sets priorities across teams.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: the CPO prioritizes across teams, and teams self-manage under their PO.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: team members are led by the PO and self-manage their tasks.

C.q: A role description states that the PM will be mentored during the project. Who is the mentor, and in which management product is this recorded?
C.why: The agile coach mentors and facilitates; role descriptions record each role's specific responsibilities, for example that the PM is mentored by the agile coach (Table 7.3).

whyNot.0: The team coach supports one or two delivery teams, not the PM.
whyNot.2: The executive approves the brief; mentoring the PM is the agile coach's work.
whyNot.3: Assurance monitors adherence; the quality management approach covers quality methods.

C.q: Who helps with research for a stakeholder analysis, and who should make sure the resulting risks are controlled?
C.why: Project support assists with stakeholder analysis and documentation, and the PM makes sure risks are identified, assessed and controlled (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The agile coach does not research stakeholder analysis, and the team coach works inside teams.
whyNot.1: Assurance confirms process and quality rather than doing the research; the CPO represents users.
whyNot.3: The PO works at team level, and the executive is accountable rather than controlling risks day to day.

C.q: An organization is early in adopting agile and staff do not yet understand the new ways of working. What should the agile coach focus on FIRST?
options: Prioritizing the user stories for each team
Training plus practical coaching on the job
Writing the communications plan for the launch
Selecting digital tools for every team
C.why: Early in a transformation the coach should build agile knowledge and skills through training and practical on-the-job coaching (2.7.3).

whyNot.0: Prioritizing user stories is not an agile coach responsibility; it belongs to the CPO and POs.
whyNot.2: Communications planning does not meet the immediate need for agile knowledge.
whyNot.3: Introducing tools before understanding does not build the mindset or skills.

reteach.title: Captain, crew office and sailing coach
reteach.question: On a sailing voyage, who steers day to day, who keeps the logbooks and supplies, and who teaches the whole fleet to sail better?

blocks.body: The captain sails the ship for the owners within agreed limits: the project manager. The crew office keeps the logs, charts and supply lists up to date: project support. A coach who works with the whole fleet, helping owners and captains change how they sail: the agile coach.

blocks.text: The fleet coach is not a member of one boat's crew. That boat-level coach is the team coach.

explain.body: Runs the project for the board within tolerances, as a servant leader. Agrees sets of user stories with POs and controls risks.

test.q: With whom does the project manager agree work package descriptions?
test.why: The PM agrees work package descriptions with product owners (Table 7.2, Table B.1).

whyNot.1: The senior supplier represents the supplier side at governance level.
whyNot.2: Team coaches support the teams but do not accept work packages.
whyNot.3: Developers receive work through their product owner, not directly from the PM.

explain.body: Admin for iterations and workshops, tools advice, planning and risk support, dashboards, lists, stakeholder analysis help, and communication between governance and teams.

test.q: A team needs someone to compile a list of open actions for the board. Which role is MOST suitable?
test.why: Compiling lists and administrative tasks are project support responsibilities (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The agile coach supports leaders with expert agile knowledge, not admin.
whyNot.1: Assurance advises and monitors; it is not responsible for administrative support.
whyNot.2: The CPO represents users and owns the project backlog.

explain.body: Mentor and facilitator for the organization. Works across teams on systemic blockers and supports the board, assurance and PM with expert knowledge.

test.q: Which roles does the agile coach support with expert knowledge of agile practices?
test.why: The agile coach supports the project board, project assurance and the project manager with expert agile knowledge (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: Developers and testers are supported by the team coach and PO.
whyNot.2: Product owners and team coaches work at team level; the agile coach does not work at team level.
whyNot.3: Project support supports others; it is not the coach's stated audience.

explain.body: Project support helps the work happen (admin, tools, dashboards). Project assurance independently checks that principles, practices and governance are being followed.

test.q: Which task belongs to project support rather than project assurance?
options: Advice and guidance on project tools
Checking impacts on the project canvas
test.why: Advice and guidance on project tools is a project support service (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: Monitoring adherence to practices is project assurance.
whyNot.1: Advising the board and PM on exception reports is project assurance.
whyNot.3: Checking impacts against the project canvas is project assurance.
